newsitem.title: HUNGARY: RWE announces new Hungary power plant plans.
newsitem.headline: RWE announces new Hungary power plant plans.

text.p: German consortium RWE Energie AG and EVS AG announced plans on Monday to build two new 500 MW power plants in Hungary but indicated the investment depended on resolving current drawn-out talks on energy prices.
"We believe the economic and political conditions in Hungary are ready for us to participate in the tender process but there are some crucial questions," RWE director Klaus Bussfeld told Reuters.

Bussfeld was speaking after signing a 47 billion forint deal with the Hungarian government on upgrading three 200 MW coal-fired units at the Matra power plant site RWE-EVS runs in north-east Hungary and extending nearby lignite mines.

The retrofit of the three existing plants forms the first part of a total 325 billion forint plan which includes building the two new lignite-powered 500 MW units, a tender for which is to be announced later this year.

The RWE-EVS consortium acquired a 38 percent stake in Matra when Hungary launched a $2 billion utility sell-off in 1995, the most far-reaching energy privatisation programme in a post-communist state.
The consortium also bought 46 percent of Budapest electricity distributor ELMU and 48 percent of regional distributor EMASZ and therefore has an interest in retail energy prices.

Since Hungary postponed retail price increases to January from last October and then introduced a quarterly price-fixing mechanism which some investors said excluded key costs, firms such as RWE, Bayernwerk and Electricite de France have been engaged in tough talks with the government.
These have centred around a commitment made by the government in an appendix to the main privatisation contracts that the pricing formula would ensure an eight percent return on investment.
"We have a lot of problems in our day-to-day business in Hungary concerning the pricing system," Bussfeld said.
"We have reached a general (pricing) agreement but...for example...debt management is not acknowledged as part of the price mechanism.
He said he hoped that the talks would succeed in a few months. The relationship with foreign investors could be in danger if there was no result by the autumn.

"If there is no reliability of the Hungarian government and parliament then there cannot be any big investments," Bussfeld said, adding that the two new lignite plants at Matra would certainly be in jeopardy without a satisfactory pricing mechanism.
He said RWE-EVS was also looking to secure a power purchase agreement with Hungarian energy supplier MVM.

The Matra investment programme represents one of the biggest foreign investments RWE has been involved in and the largest such programme in any of the ten countries applying to join the European Union (EU), the company said.
"Hungary could play a leading role in central Europe by transforming the structure of its energy supply and by building new power plants which comply with EU requirements," Bussfeld told reporters.

Earlier on Monday, British generator Powergen Plc said it had secured a long-term power purchase agreement in Hungary, paving the way for the development of a 160 million pound ($261 million) power plant in Budapest.
